blocks.text: I can take part in a full {debate}.
In this lesson, you will be taking part in a full debate.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A person in charge of a meeting, event, discussion or debate.
A person who measures or records the amount of time taken during an event.
A brief attempted interruption of someone’s speech.
A counter-argument made against something specific that the opposing team has said.

blocks.text: In a debate there are these roles: speakers, summary speakers, floor speakers, a chairperson, a timekeeper and judge(s). Don’t forget the audience: they play an important role too! Tap each role.

items.def: Make the speeches for their team.
Help the speakers to prepare for the debate, and can speak during the floor debate section.
Directs and keeps order in the debate. They introduce each speaker and explain to the audience what is happening.
Monitors the time of each speech.
Score the debate and decide the winning team.
Watch the debate, ask questions in the floor debate section and may vote for a winning team.

blocks.q: Read what each person does. Which role are they?

items.q: Maya keeps track of how long each speaker has spoken and signals when they are in or out of protected time.
Sam scores the debate using criteria and decides the winning team.
Lee helps a speaker prepare their speech and can speak during the floor debate.
Priya introduces each speaker and keeps order in the debate.

blocks.text: The number of speakers in a debate can vary depending on how large the total group of people is. Usually, a debate team consists of:
When each speaker is preparing their speech, a floor speaker can support them: discussing ideas and practising saying parts of the speech aloud.
Anyone who is not in one of the roles will be part of the audience.
The order of a debate is set and always remains the same. The chairperson introduces each speaker and explains to the audience what is happening.

items: 1. Speaker 1 for the proposition
2. Speaker 1 for the opposition
3. Speaker 2 for the proposition
4. Speaker 2 for the opposition
5. Speaker 3 for the proposition
6. Speaker 3 for the opposition
7. Floor debate
8. Summary speaker for the opposition
9. Summary speaker for the proposition

blocks.text: The order alternates throughout, with the proposition going first each time. After the floor debate, the order switches and the opposition summary speaker goes first.

blocks.label: Tap: what happens in the floor debate?
blocks.text: The floor speakers make their suggestions. They can make very small speeches if they have a point prepared that they want to raise. The audience can also ask questions to the speakers in this section.

blocks.q: Use the order of a full debate.

items.q: Who speaks straight after Speaker 2 for the proposition?
Who makes the very last speech of the whole debate?
Who speaks first: Speaker 1 for the proposition or Speaker 1 for the opposition?

blocks.text: A debate is usually judged so that there is a winning team. It can be judged in several ways:

items: by the audience voting on which team they felt was the most convincing (a show of hands)
by a single judge using their own opinion or a scoring criteria
by a panel of judges using a scoring criteria

blocks.text: Speakers may be scored on criteria such as:

items: style
content
delivery
points of information

blocks.text: Next lesson, you will review your own performance. It helps to record the whole debate so you can watch yourselves and reflect on, review and score your own performance.
While a speaker is making their speech, the opposing team’s speakers can interrupt them by challenging them with a **point of information**.
A point of information is a brief attempted interruption by the opposing team during a team’s speech.
It can be phrased as a question. This works well because it puts pressure on the speaker to answer.
To make a point of information, a member of the opposing team needs to:

items: stand up
put one hand on their head
extend one hand out towards the speaker

blocks.text: Points of information can only be made during unprotected time, and they should be 10 to 15 seconds long.
During a speaker’s speech, the first thirty seconds and the last thirty seconds are {protected time}. Points of information cannot be made then.
The timekeeper signals when a speaker is in or out of protected time.

blocks.q: In a debate where each speech is three minutes long, can the opposing team make a point of information at this moment?

items.q: The speaker has been speaking for 20 seconds.
The speaker has been speaking for 1 minute 15 seconds.
The speaker has been speaking for 2 minutes 45 seconds.

blocks.label: Tap to see how to work it out
blocks.text: Protected time is the first 30 seconds (0:00 to 0:30) and the last 30 seconds (2:30 to 3:00) of a three-minute speech. 20 seconds and 2 minutes 45 seconds are both protected. 1 minute 15 seconds is in unprotected time, so a point of information is allowed.
A rebuttal is a counter-argument made against something specific that the opposing team has said.

items: A speaker can make a rebuttal at the very beginning of their speech, before they say their own point.
A rebuttal should be around 15 to 20 seconds long, so the speaker does not use up too much of their speaking time.
A rebuttal works well when it is phrased as a question: the opposing team cannot answer because it is not their turn to speak, and not answering will make them appear weak.

blocks.text: Speakers should always listen carefully to the opposing team, to listen out for opportunities to make a rebuttal against them.
A point of information is similar to a rebuttal: both are short, and both work well phrased as a question. The difference is when they are made.

blocks.q: Tap a sentence, then tap the column it belongs in.

items.text: Made by a member of the opposing team while you are speaking
Made at the very beginning of your own speech, before your own point
Can only be made out of protected time
Should be around 15 to 20 seconds long

blocks.text: The audience is involved in the debate by:

items: watching the speeches and reacting appropriately
asking questions to the speakers during the floor debate section
voting by a show of hands to decide the winning team (if judges are not being used)

blocks.text: Being a member of the audience can also be a great way to be introduced to debating, if you are not ready for one of the more prominent roles.
It is very normal to feel nervous when public speaking. To overcome nervousness, you may wish to:

items: take deep breaths before you start speaking to calm yourself
keep positive and visualise how well your speech is going to go
find a friendly face in the audience and start by delivering your speech to them

blocks.text: More top tips: use facial expressions and gestures, stand up straight, speak in a loud, clear voice, make eye contact, keep your feet grounded and flat on the floor, and introduce yourself when you start speaking and thank the audience when you’re finished.

blocks.q: Just before your speech, your nerves start to rise. Which is a good thing to try?
options: take deep breaths to calm yourself
speak as quietly as you can
blocks.why: Taking deep breaths calms you. Visualise your speech going well, not badly, and speak in a loud, clear voice.

blocks.text: Before you start, make sure you know:

items: How many speakers will each team have?
How long will each speaker have to speak?
Does everyone know what role they are fulfilling?
How is the debate being judged?

blocks.text: Then check you have:

items: decided a motion
split into two teams: proposition and opposition
appointed speakers, summary speakers and floor speakers
appointed people to the roles of chairperson and timekeeper
decided how the debate will be judged

blocks.text: After your debate, ask yourself: Did you enjoy debating? Is there anything you could have done better? Listen to feedback from the audience.

items: A debate can be led by a {chairperson} who introduces the speakers and keeps order.
A debate is timed by a {timekeeper} so that each speaker has the same amount of time to speak.
A {point of information} is a brief attempted interruption of someone’s speech and is similar to {rebuttal}.

flashcards.front: What does the chairperson do in a debate?
flashcards.back: Directs and keeps order in the debate, introduces each speaker and explains to the audience what is happening.
Monitors the time of each speech, so that each speaker has the same amount of time to speak. They signal when a speaker is in or out of protected time.

flashcards.front: What is a point of information?
flashcards.back: A brief attempted interruption of someone’s speech by the opposing team.
A counter-argument made against something specific that the opposing team has said.

flashcards.front: What does a floor speaker do?
flashcards.back: Helps the speakers prepare for the debate, and can speak during the floor debate section.
Score the debate and decide the winning team.

flashcards.front: How is the audience involved in a debate?
flashcards.back: They watch the speeches, ask questions during the floor debate section, and may vote by a show of hands if judges are not being used.

flashcards.front: Usually, what does a debate team consist of?
flashcards.back: 3 speakers, 1 summary speaker and 4 floor speakers. The number can vary depending on how large the group is.

flashcards.front: In the order of a debate, which team speaks first each time, and what changes after the floor debate?
flashcards.back: The proposition goes first each time. After the floor debate, the order switches: the opposition summary speaker goes first.

flashcards.front: What three things must you do to make a point of information?
flashcards.back: Stand up, put one hand on your head and extend one hand out towards the speaker.

flashcards.front: How long should a point of information be, and when can it be made?
flashcards.back: 10 to 15 seconds, during unprotected time only.
The first thirty seconds and the last thirty seconds of a speaker’s speech. Points of information cannot be made then.

flashcards.front: When can a speaker make a rebuttal, and how long should it be?
flashcards.back: At the very beginning of their speech, before their own point. It should be around 15 to 20 seconds.

flashcards.front: Why does it work well to phrase a rebuttal as a question?
flashcards.back: The opposing team cannot answer because it is not their turn to speak, and not answering makes them appear weak.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Holding a full debate
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word, a number or a short phrase.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a brief attempted interruption of someone’s speech by the opposing team?
questions.explanation: A point of information is a brief attempted interruption of someone’s speech.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a counter-argument made against something specific that the opposing team has said?
questions.explanation: A rebuttal is a counter-argument against something specific that the opposing team has said.

questions.prompt: Which role measures the time each speaker takes and signals when they are in or out of protected time?
questions.explanation: The timekeeper monitors the time of each speech.

questions.prompt: How many seconds at the start of a speech, and the same number at the end, are protected time?
questions.explanation: The first thirty seconds and the last thirty seconds of a speech are protected time.

questions.prompt: After the floor debate, which team’s summary speaker speaks first: the proposition or the opposition?
questions.explanation: The order switches after the floor debate, so the opposition summary speaker goes first.

questions.prompt: Usually, how many floor speakers does a debate team have? (a number)
questions.explanation: A debate team usually has 3 speakers, 1 summary speaker and 4 floor speakers.

questions.prompt: Which section of a debate takes place after the speeches, where floor speakers can raise points and the audience can ask questions?
questions.explanation: The floor debate takes place after the speakers’ speeches, and before the summary speakers.

questions.prompt: Which role scores each speaker using criteria to decide the winning team? (one word)
questions.explanation: Judges score the debate and decide the winning team.

questions.prompt: A rebuttal should be around 15 to 20 seconds long. What is the longest it should be, in seconds?
questions.explanation: A rebuttal should be short so that the speaker does not use up too much of their own speaking time: 20 seconds is the maximum.
